title: Alive
description: Pearl Jam's debut single from Ten, built on Stone Gossard's pre-band demo riff and Eddie Vedder's semi-autobiographical lyric about a boy learning the truth about his father.

pops.text: The music came first: guitarist Stone Gossard wrote it before Pearl Jam even had a singer — it was on the demo tape that went hunting for one.
The singer hunt ended in San Diego: Eddie Vedder got the tape, wrote lyrics in the surf, and mailed back his vocals.
'Alive' is part one of Vedder's 'Mammasan' trilogy — with 'Once' and 'Footsteps' — one dark story told across three songs.
The lyric is semi-autobiographical: Vedder learned as a teen that the man he called Dad was his stepfather — and that his real father had already died.
From the 1991 debut album Ten — named for basketball player Mookie Blaylock's jersey number. The band was briefly even called Mookie Blaylock.
Released as a single in January 1992, it climbed to #16 on Billboard's Mainstream Rock chart.
It hit #16 in the UK too — Pearl Jam were a word-of-mouth live sensation before US pop radio fully caught on.
Vedder says the fans flipped the song's meaning: a crowd roaring 'I'm still alive' turned a heavy lyric into a celebration — he calls it lifting the curse.
That soaring solo is Mike McCready channeling his two biggest heroes, Jimi Hendrix and Stevie Ray Vaughan.
Three decades on, it's still a fixture of nearly every Pearl Jam show — and the mass singalong is the point now.

title: Jeremy
description: Pearl Jam's harrowing Ten single inspired by a real Texas school tragedy, with Mark Pellington's award-winning video — presented here in its uncensored 4K cut.

pops.text: Bassist Jeff Ament wrote the music and demoed it on a 12-string bass — that's the chiming low end running under everything.
Vedder wrote the lyric after reading a short newspaper item about Jeremy Wade Delle, a 15-year-old from Richardson, Texas, who shot himself in front of his English class in January 1991.
He folded in a memory of his own: a junior-high classmate who brought a gun to school and fired into a classroom.
Director Mark Pellington shot the video in London, intercutting the band with actor Trevor Wilson as Jeremy.
MTV heavily edited the original cut — the most shocking shot was removed. The current 4K upload restores Pellington's uncensored version.
The video won four awards at the 1993 MTV VMAs, including Video of the Year.
Accepting the award, Vedder suggested that without music, he might have ended up on a similar path himself.
Chart check: #5 on Billboard's Mainstream Rock chart and #15 in the UK — powered by airplay alone, since it wasn't sold as a US commercial single.
That frozen final stare became one of the most iconic images in '90s music video.
Same director, different NC band: Mark Pellington also directed The Connells' '74-'75' video — it's in this batch too.

title: Tonight, Tonight
description: The Smashing Pumpkins' orchestral Mellon Collie single, paired with a Méliès-inspired silent-film fantasy video that swept the 1996 MTV VMAs.

pops.text: Billy Corgan has called this his Cheap Trick tribute — 'dark optimism': a bleak lyric wrapped in a euphoric wall of sound.
Those strings are real: a 30-piece section drawn from the Chicago Symphony Orchestra, arranged and conducted by Audrey Riley.
Corgan and Riley argued for four days over the string arrangement — he wanted it huge, and recorded it with no click track to rein it in.
The video is a love letter to Georges Méliès' 1902 silent film A Trip to the Moon — the album cover reminded the directors of early silent-film art.

Directors Jonathan Dayton and Valerie Faris scrapped their first concept — Busby Berkeley divers splashing into champagne glasses — because the Red Hot Chili Peppers had just done nearly the same thing for 'Aeroplane.'
The star sailors are Tom Kenny and Jill Talley — a married comedy duo who later became the voices of SpongeBob SquarePants and his computer wife, Karen.
The handmade moonscapes and puppets came from production designer Wayne White, who'd won Emmys designing Pee-wee's Playhouse.
From the 1995 double album Mellon Collie and the Infinite Sadness — 28 tracks that debuted at #1.
The video swept the 1996 MTV Video Music Awards with six wins, including Breakthrough Video.
Released as a single in May 1996, it remains the Pumpkins' signature orchestral moment.

title: Today
description: Siamese Dream's deceptively sunny single — an ice-cream-truck melody built over the darkest lyric Billy Corgan had ever written.

pops.text: The cheeriest-sounding song on Siamese Dream was written at Billy Corgan's lowest point — broke, depressed, and having suicidal thoughts.
He wrote it in about ten minutes. The opening riff arrived unplanned in rehearsal — Corgan calls it a 'chiming clock of anticipation.'
So the ice-cream-truck sweetness is deliberate irony: the happiest melody he could build, over the darkest lyric he'd written.
Corgan plays the ice-cream man in the video — check the name tag: it reads 'Billie.'
Director Stéphane Sednaoui shot the video on cheap photo equipment on purpose — the faded, washed-out look is a style choice, not a budget problem.
The desert wanderings were filmed at Zabriskie Point in Death Valley — a nod to Antonioni's 1970 film of the same name.
Behind the scenes the band was fracturing: Jimmy Chamberlin's heroin addiction and James Iha and D'arcy Wretzky's breakup shadowed the whole Siamese Dream era.
Second single from Siamese Dream, released in September 1993 — the song that moved the Pumpkins from cult act to MTV rotation.
It peaked at #4 on Billboard's Modern Rock Tracks, their biggest US radio hit of the era.
Corgan later said the 'greatest day' line was an act of will — daring himself to believe it for three minutes.

title: My Name Is Mud
description: Pork Soda's lead single: Les Claypool's slap-bass murder ballad, narrated by a backwoods killer calmly digging a grave.

pops.text: Meet Mud: a backwoods ne'er-do-well who beats his friend to death with a baseball bat — and narrates the whole song while digging the grave.
That's Claypool's slap bass doing the singing — he plays a six-string fretless Carl Thompson bass fitted with a whammy bar.
From 1993's Pork Soda — which somehow debuted at #7 on the Billboard 200, quite possibly the weirdest album ever to crash the Top 10.
Pork Soda's murky mood had a cause: the band was fried from nonstop touring, and Claypool has said the darkness came straight from that headspace.
At Woodstock '94 the crowd pelted the stage with mud during this very song — Claypool stopped to scold them, then played on.
If fans at a Primus show chant 'Primus sucks!' it's a compliment — the band started the joke themselves on their first live album, Suck on This.
Guitarist Larry 'Ler' LaLonde was a student of Joe Satriani — and as a teenager played in the death-metal band Possessed.
Drummer Tim 'Herb' Alexander's kick-drum work here is why prog drummers cite a funk-metal band as an influence.
Claypool once auditioned to replace Cliff Burton in Metallica. They passed — and he went home and built Primus instead.
The video puts Claypool in Mud's overalls, stone-faced, while the band churns behind him. Deadpan was always Primus' best special effect.

title: Jerry Was a Race Car Driver
description: Primus' major-label breakthrough from Sailing the Seas of Cheese — a two-character tragedy about a doomed racer and a forcibly retired fireman.

pops.text: Primus' major-label breakthrough: the first single from 1991's Sailing the Seas of Cheese.
Jerry 'drove so goddamned fast, never did win no checkered flags, but he never did come in last' — Claypool builds the whole tragedy in one chorus.
That cackling sample — 'Dog will hunt!' — is Chop Top, Bill Moseley's character from The Texas Chainsaw Massacre 2.
Verse two flips to Captain Pierce, a Richmond fireman forced into retirement at 65 — and it 'stuck in his craw.'
The video, directed by Mark Kohr, is live footage shot at the Phoenix Theater in Petaluma, California — pure hometown Primus energy.
It peaked at #23 on Billboard's Modern Rock Tracks in 1991 — the song that took 'Primus sucks' nationwide.
Jerry's ride is a '442' — the Oldsmobile muscle car — complete with a 'Bocephus' sticker, Hank Williams Jr.'s nickname.
A whole generation met Primus here, via the first Tony Hawk's Pro Skater soundtrack in 1999.
The past tense in the title is the spoiler: Jerry, 22, has one too many cold beers and wraps himself around a telephone pole.
It's also playable in Rock Band 3. Good luck with that bassline on Expert.

title: Under the Bridge
description: Blood Sugar Sex Magik's aching ballad — Anthony Kiedis' poem about loneliness and addiction in Los Angeles, directed by Gus Van Sant.

pops.text: This began as a poem in Anthony Kiedis' notebook — producer Rick Rubin found it while flipping through and pushed him to show the band.
Kiedis felt like the odd man out: Flea and John Frusciante would go off together, and he — newly sober — was alone in Los Angeles.
The 'city of angels' is L.A. itself, and the bridge is a real one downtown, where Kiedis used to score and use heroin.
He has never publicly identified which bridge it is. Fans nominate candidates; Kiedis keeps it private on purpose.
From 1991's Blood Sugar Sex Magik, recorded with Rick Rubin at The Mansion in Laurel Canyon — a house once leased by Harry Houdini.
That gospel swell at the end? Frusciante's mother, Gail, and her church-choir friends sang the backing vocals.
The video was directed by Gus Van Sant — a few years before Good Will Hunting — shooting the band around downtown L.A.
It peaked at #2 on the Billboard Hot 100, the Chili Peppers' biggest pop hit of their lives to that point.
In the UK it needed a second push — a 1994 re-release took it to #13.
Kiedis nearly kept the poem to himself: he thought it was too personal, and too soft, for a Chili Peppers record. Rubin disagreed. Rubin was right.

title: Californication
description: The title track of the Chili Peppers' 1999 comeback album, with the band dropped into a fictional open-world video game that ends in an earthquake.

pops.text: Welcome to the video game that isn't: directors Jonathan Dayton and Valerie Faris turned the band into avatars in a fake open-world game.
Same directing duo as the Smashing Pumpkins' 'Tonight, Tonight' video — also in this batch.
The song is Kiedis' travelogue of a planet going plastic: from Sweden to Alaska, everywhere is becoming California.
'Psychic spies from China try to steal your mind's elation' — the lyric is a collage of images about fame and the American dream curdling.
From the 1999 album Californication — guitarist John Frusciante's return after six years away, and the record that relaunched the band.
As a single in June 2000 it topped both the Mainstream Rock and Modern Rock charts for weeks — while only reaching #69 on the Hot 100. Rock radio owned this one.
Every band member gets a character-select screen and a stats readout — Flea's avatar surfs, snowboards and generally defies physics.
The finale: an earthquake levels the whole gamescape as the band regroups at the center of the Earth.
Uploaded to YouTube in October 2009, the video passed one billion views in 2022 — the band's first to do it.
Frusciante's guitar figure here is minimalism as a flex: two notes doing the work of an orchestra.

title: Touch of Grey
description: The Grateful Dead's only Top 10 single and their famous skeleton video — filmed with a live audience at Laguna Seca, it made the Dead MTV stars 22 years in.

pops.text: The song that finally broke the Grateful Dead on MTV — twenty-two years into their career.
Jerry Garcia and Robert Hunter wrote it, and the band had been playing it live since 1982 before it ever reached a studio.
The video was filmed in front of a live audience after a show at Laguna Seca Raceway in May 1987 — the crowd stuck around to watch the band turn into skeletons.
Director Gary Gutierrez had form: he'd animated sequences for The Grateful Dead Movie a decade earlier, in 1977.
The skeleton look nods to Stanley Mouse and Alton Kelley's famous 1966 'Skeleton and Roses' concert poster.
Garcia was only 44 in this video — the grey beard made him rock's favorite grandfather a generation early.
It became the Dead's ONLY Top 10 single: #9 on the Hot 100 and #1 on the Mainstream Rock chart.
Parent album In the Dark was likewise their only Top 10 album — recorded on a dim theater stage, playing in near-darkness to fake the live feel.
The flood of new young fans it brought in got a nickname: 'Touchheads.' Some old Deadheads grumbled; the band cashed the checks.
After Garcia's 1986 diabetic coma, the Dead opened their comeback show with this song. 'I will get by, I will survive' landed like a promise.

title: Hell in a Bucket
description: In the Dark's other video: a pastel-clad Bob Weir walks into a biker bar full of devils, circus folk and one very relaxed duck.

pops.text: Bob Weir takes the lead vocal — he co-wrote it with lyricist John Perry Barlow and keyboardist Brent Mydland.
The video is pure 1987: Weir, in full pastel Miami Vice mode, strolls into a biker bar staffed by devils.
Yes, that is a duck sitting at the bar, drinking. Nobody in the band has ever adequately explained the duck.
Phil Lesh pops up dressed as a circus ringleader — because of course he does.
One of the dancing devils is Trixie Garcia — Jerry Garcia's daughter.
Director Len Dell'Amico was the Dead's longtime video collaborator, shooting much of their official live footage.
From In the Dark, released July 6, 1987 — the album that turned the Dead, impossibly, into MTV-era hitmakers.
'At least I'm enjoying the ride' — Barlow's lyric shrugs cheerfully straight into the flames.
Like most of In the Dark, it had been a live staple for years before the band finally recorded it.
Co-writer Brent Mydland, twinkling away on the keys here, was the Dead's longest-tenured keyboardist — nobody else held that chair as long.

title: Paint It, Black
description: The Stones' sitar-driven 1966 chart-topper — a funeral-dark single that hit #1 on both sides of the Atlantic and helped launch rock's raga craze.

pops.text: Released in May 1966 — and it went to #1 in both the US and the UK.
That exotic drone is Brian Jones on sitar — he'd picked up the instrument after hearing George Harrison use one on 'Norwegian Wood.'
It started in the studio as a jokey, slow funeral-parlor take, with Bill Wyman fooling around on the organ pedals — then the band doubled the tempo and it turned sinister.
The comma in 'Paint It, Black' was a Decca Records typo. Mick Jagger decided it changed the meaning — and it stayed.
Jagger and Richards wrote it; in America it opened the US version of the Aftermath album.
Charlie Watts drives the whole record with that relentless gallop — cut at RCA Studios in Hollywood in March 1966.
Rolling Stone magazine ranks it #174 on its list of the 500 Greatest Songs of All Time.
This is ABKCO's official lyric video — the Stones never made a promo film for it in '66, so the words do all the haunting.
It's been scoring darkness ever since — from the end credits of Full Metal Jacket to Wednesday Addams' cello practice.
Jones' sitar helped kick off rock's brief raga craze — within a year, everybody was droning.

title: Start Me Up
description: Tattoo You's lead single — a 1978 Some Girls outtake that began life as a reggae song, sat in the vault for three years, then became an era-defining hit.

pops.text: This monster hit sat in a drawer for three years — it was recorded in Paris in early 1978, during the Some Girls sessions.
And it began life as a reggae song called 'Never Stop' — the band cut take after take of it as reggae and shelved them all.
Keith Richards says that somewhere in those sessions they also cut two straight rock takes — and take two was the keeper.
Engineer Chris Kimsey rediscovered the rock take in 1981 while mining the vaults for Tattoo You — an album built largely from leftovers.
Released August 14, 1981, it roared to #2 on the Hot 100, held off the top by Christopher Cross's 'Arthur's Theme.'
It went #1 in Australia and #7 in the UK — not bad for a three-year-old outtake.
The B-side was 'No Use in Crying,' a slow Tattoo You ballad — one single, both ends of the Stones.
This promo video is peak '81 Stones: Mick strutting, the band pretending the song is brand new.
Fourteen years later it launched Windows 95 — Microsoft reportedly paid around $3 million to pair it with the Start button.
The leftovers trick worked: Tattoo You hit #1, and 'Start Me Up' has been kicking off Stones shows ever since.

title: Losing My Religion
description: R.E.M.'s breakthrough hit from Out of Time — a mandolin-driven song about unrequited love whose title is Southern slang for losing your temper.

pops.text: Peter Buck wrote that famous riff on a mandolin he'd just bought — he taped himself practicing while watching TV and liked this bit the next day.
'Losing my religion' is a Southern expression for losing your temper or your civility — the song is about unrequited love, not faith.
Michael Stipe has described it as his take on an obsessive crush, in the vein of The Police's 'Every Breath You Take.'
Released February 19, 1991 as the lead single from Out of Time, it became R.E.M.'s biggest US hit, peaking at #4 on the Hot 100.
Director Tarsem Singh filled the video with Caravaggio-style imagery and echoes of Gabriel García Márquez's story 'A Very Old Man with Enormous Wings.'
Stipe lip-synchs in this video — something he'd vowed never to do — because Tarsem convinced him the film needed it.
The video won six awards at the 1991 MTV VMAs including Video of the Year, plus the Grammy for Best Short Form Music Video.
Out of Time went on to sell more than 18 million copies worldwide — the mandolin riff heard round the world.
In 2020, this became the first R.E.M. video to pass one billion views on YouTube.
The song entered the Grammy Hall of Fame in 2017.

title: Everybody Hurts
description: Automatic for the People's consoling ballad — written mostly by drummer Bill Berry, with strings arranged by Led Zeppelin's John Paul Jones.

pops.text: The unlikeliest R.E.M. song story: drummer Bill Berry wrote most of this one — and then barely plays on it.
Berry's seat is taken by a vintage Univox drum machine; he 'performs' on the track through a drum pattern he sampled himself.
Those lush strings were arranged by John Paul Jones — yes, Led Zeppelin's bassist, moonlighting as an orchestrator.
From 1992's Automatic for the People — Stipe aimed the lyric squarely at struggling teenagers: hold on.
The video, directed by Jake Scott, strands the band in a traffic jam filmed near San Antonio, Texas, with strangers' thoughts appearing as subtitles.
Released as a single in April 1993, it reached #29 in the US but went Top 10 in the UK, Canada, France, Ireland and beyond.
In 2010, a star-studded charity cover of it raised money for Haiti earthquake relief — and topped the UK chart.
Q magazine ranked it #31 on its list of the '1001 Best Songs Ever.'
The album title is the slogan of Weaver D's, a soul-food restaurant in the band's hometown of Athens, Georgia: 'Automatic for the People.'
Berry left R.E.M. in 1997, two years after suffering a brain aneurysm on stage. The band continued as a trio — they never replaced him.

title: Come Together
description: Abbey Road's swampy opener — written by Lennon as a campaign song for Timothy Leary, built on McCartney's bass riff and Ringo's tom-toms.

pops.text: John Lennon wrote this as a campaign song for Timothy Leary, who was running for governor of California against Ronald Reagan.
Leary's slogan was 'Come together, join the party.' When the campaign collapsed, Lennon kept the phrase and built this instead.
'Here come ol' flat-top' was borrowed from Chuck Berry's 'You Can't Catch Me' — it later landed Lennon in a legal fight, settled partly with his Rock 'n' Roll covers album.
Recorded in July 1969 — take 6 became the master. That's Paul's liquid bass and Ringo's swampy tom-toms carrying the whole record.
The whispered 'shoot me' over handclaps opens every verse — listen for Lennon harmonizing with himself on the outro.
Producer George Martin said that if he had to pick one track showing how the four disparate Beatles combined into something greater, he'd pick this one.
Abbey Road's opening track, released September 26, 1969 — it topped the US chart as a double A-side with George's 'Something.'
In the UK it peaked at #4 — the Beatles rarely released singles at home by then, which makes this a late oddity.
This official video arrived in 2015, when Apple remastered the Beatles' promo clips for the '1+' collection.
Lennon's own review: 'It's funky, it's bluesy... I'd buy it!'

title: Here Comes the Sun
description: George Harrison's Abbey Road jewel — written in Eric Clapton's garden while playing hooky from Apple, and now the Beatles' most-streamed song.

pops.text: George Harrison wrote this in Eric Clapton's garden in Surrey — he'd played hooky from Apple's business meetings to go and sit in the sun.
His words: Apple had become 'like school... sign this and sign that.' One spring morning he picked up one of Clapton's acoustics, and the song just came.
John Lennon doesn't play on this track at all — he was recovering from a car crash when the backing track was cut.
That's Harrison on a Moog synthesizer, too — the instrument was brand new in Britain, and the Beatles had gotten hold of one of the first.
Recorded across July and August 1969 at Abbey Road, with an uncredited little orchestra of violas, cellos, flutes and clarinets swelling underneath.
It's the most-streamed Beatles song of the streaming era — the first of their songs to pass a billion plays on Spotify.
Harrison was still the 'junior' songwriter, rationed to about two songs per album. On Abbey Road, his two — this and 'Something' — stole the show.
This official video finally arrived fifty years later, premiering September 26, 2019, for Abbey Road's anniversary.
Directors Alasdair Brotherston and Jock Mooney built it from Linda McCartney's photos and footage of the band's final photoshoot at Tittenhurst Park.
The closing sun is assembled, shot by shot, above Ringo's drum kit in Studio Two. Half a century on — still a sunrise.

title: Sultans of Swing
description: Dire Straits' debut single — Mark Knopfler's portrait of a defiant pub jazz band, carried by one of the most admired guitar performances in rock.

pops.text: Mark Knopfler wrote this after watching a mediocre Dixieland jazz band in a nearly empty Deptford pub — who grandly announced themselves as 'the Sultans of Swing.'
He thought the song was dull — until he played it on his first Fender Stratocaster, a '61, and, in his words, 'it just came alive.'
The original demo, cut in July 1977, got played on BBC Radio London — within two months, Phonogram Records offered the band a deal.
'Guitar George' and Harry with the daytime job are portraits of that pub band itself — weekend warriors with no illusions left.
Re-recorded in February 1978 for the debut album, produced by Muff Winwood — Steve Winwood's brother.
It climbed to #4 in the US and #8 in the UK — a six-minute, solo-laden debut single that broke every rule of 1978 radio.
Knopfler plays fingerstyle, with no pick — that's how the guitar is made to 'cry or sing' with that bell-like Strat tone.
The outro solo is regularly voted among the greatest guitar solos ever recorded — all feel, zero shredding.
This official video intercuts the young band performing — Knopfler's red Strat already front and center.
The band's name was a joke about their finances — they really were in dire straits. This song fixed that.

title: Walk of Life
description: Brothers in Arms' sunniest single — a tribute to a subway busker named Johnny, with a US video built entirely from sports bloopers.

pops.text: This is about Johnny, a busker singing oldies down in the subway tunnels, 'trying to make it pay' — Knopfler's tribute to every street musician.
Johnny's setlist is name-checked in the lyric: 'Be-Bop-A-Lula,' 'I Got a Woman,' 'What'd I Say' — a whole rock'n'roll history in one verse.
Two official videos exist! This US version, stuffed with sports bloopers and directed by Stephen Johnson, was Knopfler's own idea.
The UK got a different video entirely: a busker dressed as Knopfler, intercut with the band performing.
From 1985's Brothers in Arms — the album that became the first ever to sell a million copies on a new format called CD.
In Europe it first appeared as the B-side of 'So Far Away' — then got promoted to a single in its own right.
As a US single in October 1985 it reached #7 on the Hot 100; in the UK, in January 1986, it climbed even higher — #2.
It's a zydeco-meets-rockabilly bounce — a deliberate left turn on an album famous for moody epics.
Brothers in Arms spent 14 weeks at #1 in the UK — this was its third single and its sunniest four minutes.
This song has since become the universal soundtrack to the blooper reel — exactly as Knopfler planned.

title: Run-Around
description: Blues Traveler's breakthrough from the album four — John Popper's harmonica-driven hit about unrequited love, with a Wizard of Oz-themed video.

pops.text: Blues Traveler's breakthrough: after three albums of cult jam-band status, this put John Popper's harmonica all over pop radio.
It's a true story — Popper wrote it about his unrequited crush on the band's original bassist, Felicia Lewis.
The Wizard of Oz-themed video fits a song about longing to get back to someone who won't have you.
From the band's fourth album — pointedly titled four — released in 1994.
It reached #8 on the Billboard Hot 100, and then refused to leave: 49 weeks on the chart, a record at the time.
Popper's harmonica rig is a bandolier vest holding twelve harmonicas — one in every key — so he can swap mid-song without looking.
It won the Grammy for Best Rock Performance by a Duo or Group with Vocal.
The band started as a high-school gag in Princeton, New Jersey — Popper and drummer Brendan Hill first teamed up for a Blues Brothers sketch.
Popper was a trumpet player until he convinced his teacher to let him switch to harmonica — by playing a harp version of 'She Blinded Me with Science.'
That opening 'midnight dreary' phone call? A quiet nod to Poe's 'The Raven.'

title: Hook
description: The most honest hit of the '90s: a Pachelbel-powered single whose lyric openly admits the words don't matter — the hook is what brings you back.

pops.text: The most honest hit of the '90s: a song that tells you, right in the lyric, that the lyric doesn't matter — the hook is what brings you back.
Popper literally sings that it doesn't matter what he says... and radio played it for months anyway. Point proven.
That stately chord progression? It's Pachelbel's Canon in D — the wedding standard — wearing a harmonica solo.
From the album four (1994); released as a single in September 1995, it reached #23 on the Hot 100.
The video fits the thesis perfectly: a viewer sits hypnotized by his television, subliminal images flickering past.
By the end, he turns the TV off and picks up a book. Popper approves of the message AND the harmonica break.
The bridge is a rapid-fire tongue-twister Popper fires off in one breathless run — karaoke's final boss.
Decades later, Emma Stone demolished Jimmy Fallon by lip-syncing this on The Tonight Show — still one of the most-watched lip syncs ever.
'Suck it in, suck it in, suck it in' — the song mocks pop's image obsession while cashing in on it, in the same breath.
Popper has said it began as an experiment: could a song about nothing, engineered purely around a hook, become a hit? It could.

title: One Big Holiday
description: My Morning Jacket's signature song from It Still Moves — the Louisville band's set-closing anthem, later the namesake of their own destination festival.

pops.text: My Morning Jacket's signature song — the set-closer that turns every show into exactly what the title says.
From 2003's It Still Moves, the Louisville band's third album and their major-label debut for ATO Records.
Jim James' cathedral reverb has humble roots: the band's early recordings were cut in a Kentucky grain silo, prized for its natural echo.
Their 2004 Bonnaroo set — a young band torching this song in the Tennessee woods — is still traded as one of the festival's great breakout moments.
At Bonnaroo 2008, they played it in the pouring rain with Metallica's Kirk Hammett guesting on guitar.
The band named its own destination festival after this song: One Big Holiday, launched in Riviera Maya, Mexico in 2014 with just 2,500 fans.
The song spends five minutes building toward one of the great twin-guitar blowouts in modern Southern rock.
For the 2016 It Still Moves reissue, James remixed and remastered the album and added ten of his original home demos.
Band-name legend: James found a discarded jacket monogrammed 'MMJ' and decided the letters stood for My Morning Jacket.
Two decades on, it's still the last song of the night more often than not. Some holidays you never come home from.

title: Ain't Life Grand
description: The title track of Widespread Panic's 1994 album — this 1997 live performance features founding guitarist Michael Houser, who died in 2002.

pops.text: Widespread Panic never made a studio video for this one — for a jam band, the live tape IS the video. This performance is from 1997, with founding guitarist Michael Houser.
Title track of the band's fourth album, Ain't Life Grand, released September 6, 1994 — their most radio-friendly record, full of songs like 'Airplane' and 'Little Kin.'
It debuted in July 1993 during a Charlottesville radio session — John Bell, Houser, Todd Nance and Domingo Ortiz road-testing it semi-acoustically.
Bell often plays mandolin on this one, giving the boogie a front-porch lilt.
It became one of the most-played songs in Panic history — for years, no more than seven shows ever passed without it.
Houser, whose stinging lead guitar drives this performance, was the band's heartbeat. He died of pancreatic cancer in 2002, at just 44.
Panic formed in Athens, Georgia in 1986 — fraternity-house jams that grew into one of America's biggest live draws without ever needing a hit single.
The album arrived just as the Grateful Dead's era was ending — and Panic inherited much of the jam-band crown.
In February 2025, the band opened guitarist Jimmy Herring's first show back after cancer treatment with this song. A benediction, basically.
'Ain't life grand?' Bell asks it like a toast, not a question — and thirty years on, it still opens encores.

description: Raleigh's own Connells and their one world-conquering song — a flop at home that hit #1 across Europe, with Mark Pellington's yearbook-photo video.

pops.text: Raleigh's own! The Connells formed in 1984 around brothers Mike and David Connell — and this is their one world-conquering song.
Mike Connell started writing it in early 1991 in his one-bedroom Raleigh apartment. He calls it 'just another failed relationship song.'
Recorded in March 1993 at Dreamland Studios in Bearsville, New York — a converted church — for the album Ring.
The video was directed by Mark Pellington — the 'Jeremy' director, also in this batch — and pairs yearbook photos of Broughton High School's Class of 1975 with the same people in 1993.
Broughton is a real Raleigh high school. Those are hometown faces, aging eighteen years in four minutes.
America shrugged: released in 1993, it never charted in the US. Europe, two years later, went completely mad for it.
In 1995 it hit #1 in Norway — for nine weeks — and Sweden, and the Top 10 in eleven European countries.
The UK took two bites: #14 in 1995, then #21 on a 1996 reissue. NME put it in their top 50 singles of 1995.
The band toured Europe with Def Leppard on the strength of it, and the song turns up in Heavy, the 1995 Liv Tyler film.
In 2015 the filmmakers tracked the class down again — 15 of the 16 video stars were still living — and shot an update: 1975, 1993 and today, in one frame.

title: Stone Cold Yesterday
description: The Connells' 1990 college-radio breakthrough — an unusually rousing power-pop opener from One Simple Word, and later the title of their first greatest-hits album.

pops.text: Before Europe called, this was the Connells' breakthrough: the 1990 college-radio hit that opens their album One Simple Word.
It was written by Mike Connell with singer Doug MacMillan — the band's two songwriting engines, splitting the difference.
It's the Connells in overdrive: where most of their songs jangle and brood, this one floors it — pure power pop.
Meet the cast: Jimmy, 'a bad dancer till he learned to shimmy,' and Betty, 'a slow burner till the work got steady.'
The 1990 video is a pure time capsule of Raleigh college rock — all chiming guitars and zero irony.
The Connells were jangle-pop heirs to R.E.M., and even shared that world's producers — including Mitch Easter on their early records.
Their beloved 1987 album Boylan Heights is named after a Raleigh neighborhood. This band wears its hometown on its sleeve.
In 2016, the band's first greatest-hits album took its name from this song: Stone Cold Yesterday: Best of The Connells.
That best-of spans sixteen singles from 1987 to 1998 — a whole career America mostly missed. Europe didn't.
'Changed her, it didn't change me' — the most singalong breakup shrug of the college-rock era.
